implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits the JavaScript runtime, so the IO instance is the Promise: then is bind (it flattens a returned promise), async/await is its syntax, and the compiler types the value a promise carries but not the failure it may reject with. Use it as the default; add fp-ts when the error channel itself must be typed and composable.
pitfalls: Promise rejections are untyped and invisible to the compiler: an unhandled rejection aborts Node and only surfaces at runtime.
Sequential awaits serialise independent work; use Promise.all (or an aggregate helper) where steps do not depend on each other.

variants.name: fp-ts Either / TaskEither
variants.idiom_name: fp-ts Either / TaskEither with chain and pipe
variants.implementation_notes: fp-ts supplies the typed monad instances TypeScript lacks: Either<E, A> for synchronous failure and TaskEither<E, A> (a lazy Task of Either) for async plus failure; chain is bind, map is map, tryCatch lifts a throwing function and pipe composes the pipeline without executing it. Choose it when errors are part of the domain contract and fp-ts is already a dependency - it is not stdlib, and its higher-kinded-type encoding is what makes the abstraction work.
pitfalls: fp-ts pipelines are lazy: nothing runs until the TaskEither is invoked (await task()), so a built-but-unexecuted value is a silent no-op.
The HKT emulation leaks into signatures; mixing fp-ts with raw promises reopens the untyped rejection channel.
